facts.claim: There was no evidence for an experienced well-being plateau above $75,000/y.
facts.quote: There was no evidence for an experienced well-being plateau above $75,000/y, contrary to some influential past research.

facts.claim: Both experienced and evaluative well-being increased linearly with log(income), with an equally steep slope for higher earners as for lower earners.
facts.quote: the present results show that both experienced and evaluative well-being increased linearly with log(income), with an equally steep slope for higher earners as for lower earners.

facts.claim: Happiness increases steadily with log(income) among happier people, and even accelerates in the happiest group.
facts.quote: Happiness increases steadily with log(income) among happier people, and even accelerates in the happiest group.

facts.claim: Emotional well-being rises with log income, but there is no further progress beyond an annual income of ~$75,000.
facts.quote: Emotional well-being also rises with log income, but there is no further progress beyond an annual income of ~$75,000.

facts.claim: High income is linked to a steady rise in life evaluation when plotted against log income.
facts.quote: When plotted against log income, life evaluation rises steadily.

rejected.claim: The overall association between income inequality and subjective well-being was almost zero and not statistically significant (pooled r = − 0. 01, 95% CI − 0. 08 to 0. 06; Q = 563. 10, I 2 = 95. 74%, p < 0. 001).
rejected.quote: The overall association between income inequality and SWB was almost zero and not statistically significant (pooled r = − 0. 01, 95% CI − 0. 08 to 0. 06; Q = 563. 10, I 2 = 95. 74%, p < 0. 001)

research.angle: While some studies show well-being continues to rise with income without a plateau, other research suggests that emotional well-being specifically may stop improving after $75,000.
research.verdict: The evidence is conflicting, with some studies showing a linear increase in well-being for all earners and others identifying a specific plateau for emotional well-being at $75,000.
research.caveat: The findings are complicated by different ways of measuring well-being, such as distinguishing between daily emotions and overall life evaluation.
